title: Trapped
content:
For six years, the home world had a reliable pulse for Dory. Every single day, without exception, her husband had looked at her and told her he loved her. It was a constant, predictable law of her universe, as certain as gravity. His love was a quiet room, a steady hand, and a lifetime of built safety.

Yet, sitting there with him in the gentle warmth of their home, the conversation turned toward the dark, unmapped terrain of her childhood. The trauma of an abused child doesn’t disappear just because adult life becomes gentle; in the warmth of his consistency, the old coldness felt even sharper.

​The memory didn’t fade with time; it just sat beneath the surface of her skin, waiting.

​Dory had been an accident of birth, a conception that forced two people into a bitter, early marriage. Her mother’s response to that trapped life was a cold, unyielding hatred. From the very beginning, Dory was entirely rejected, passed through the uncaring hands of orphanages and two separate foster homes. But the deepest scars were carved in the quiet darkness of a lonely apartment in Oakland, California.

​At only six years old, Dory already carried the crushing weight of a grown woman’s grief. Her world was defined by waiting in the darkness for her mother to return late at night. Her primary responsibility was protecting her younger sister, Marie. The cruelty of the rejection crystallized in the moments the front door finally clicked open. Her mother would step across the threshold, immediately gathering Marie into a warm, loving hug. When Dory stepped forward, yearning for the same warmth, she was always shoved aside—unwanted, like a stray dog left out in the rain.

​She learned early that the sharp, hollow ache of an empty stomach was easier to bear than the emotional devastation of being hated by the person who gave her life. She was never lovingly touched, held, or cuddled. What she knew was different, ugly, and a burden to her mother.

​The apex of the terror came on the nights her mother brought male companions home. To ensure no one would discover that a child was left behind alone, her mother resorted to a clinical, horrifying routine. She would pull the heavy wall bed down, stuff six-year-old Dory into the dark, cramped cavity behind it, and slam the bed back up into the wall. Trapped in the suffocating, dusty void, Dory would cry, gasping for air and clawing at the dark until she finally fell asleep.

​When she turned seven, the abandonment became absolute. Her mother took Marie and Dory to an orphanage nearby and dropped them there like a package at the door. Over the next seven years, she visited them only twice, bringing a gift only for Marie, and none for Dory.

​Stranded in the institution, Dory took out all her anger on the other children, earning a bad reputation and receiving a beating usually before bedtime every evening for seven years.

​But when she was thirteen, a brief flicker of hope arrived. Some Christian students came to tell them about Jesus. As they were leaving, one of them said, “Children, even if you forget everything else we have told you, remember God loves you.” Sitting on a folding chair in the parlor, Dory prayed for the first time in her life. She told God that if he loved her and wanted her, he could have her. On that special day, she thought she became a Christian. “I knew I was received by God,” she would later say. “At last, I had a friend, a friend forever.”

​But little did she realize, for the first time in her life outside the orphanage, that the world would be far worse for her than it was within the walls.

​She was shunted to four different foster homes. In two of them, she was physically, mentally, and sexually abused. Yet, the religious narrative she had been handed insisted that the God who was with her during her closing days in the orphanage stood with her still.

​Now, sitting across from her husband, the teacup rattled against its saucer as Dory set it down. The house was quiet, but her eyes were fixed on the wall, staring right through the present into the dark.

​”They told me He was a warrior,” Dory said, her voice dropping to a harsh, skin-scraping whisper. “Those students gave me a book filled with a God who breaks things to save the people who cry out to Him. He is the Lord who parted the Red Sea to swallow an entire Egyptian army. He commanded the sun to stand still for Joshua. He shut the mouths of starved lions for Daniel, and stood in the blazing Babylonian furnace so Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego walked out without even the smell of smoke. He sent an earthquake to shatter the foundations of a prison to free Paul and Silas.”

​She turned her gaze to her husband, her eyes fiercely, terribly awake.

​”If He could rip open the sea, manipulate the cosmos, tame wild beasts, cool the molecular heat of fire, and shatter prison iron—then stopping the hands of vile men in a foster home should have required less than a whisper. Why didn’t He? If He could part the ocean for a million strangers, why couldn’t He just lock a bedroom door for one little girl who trusted Him?”

​Her husband didn’t offer a platitude. He just held her gaze, letting the heavy truth sit between them.

​”The typical answer,” Dory whispered, her jaw tightening, “is that He was suffering with me. But that is a lie for cowards. A friend who stands by and watches you get broken because it’s part of some grand, invisible equation isn’t a friend at all. That is an accomplice.”

​She looked down at her hands, the illusion finally shattering completely under the weight of honest psychology.

​”This God is no better than an imaginary friend,” she said, the words cutting through the quiet room like a scalpel. “The psychology says that when you fear and go through immense trauma that your brain cannot bear, so in order to protect itself from going insane and losing the grasp of reality, it creates an imaginary situation or a person or anything imaginary where it can feel the comfort and love and all the lackings that it that a person is not receiving. So what is to say that God is just an imaginary construct or any better than that?”

​She looked at her husband, the clinical truth giving her a cold, unbreakable clarity.

​”It’s called structural dissociation. My brain fractured itself to keep me from shattering. It created a fantasy defense—an inner sanctuary with an imaginary guardian—because the alternative was total psychological death. My cognitive architecture was just trying to detect a protector in an empty room because it was hardwired to survive. It wasn’t the Holy Spirit visiting a thirteen-year-old girl; it was a traumatized ego deploying every defense mechanism it had left.”

​She let out a long, slow breath, her shoulders dropping as the ancient, cosmic guilt poured out of her.

​”I didn’t survive because of a miracle,” Dory said, looking her husband dead in the eye, finally claiming her own immense, terrifying strength. “My brain did what it had to do to keep that little girl in the wall bed from breaking. He didn’t keep me safe. I kept me safe. My own mind fought for me until I was strong enough to walk out of the dark and find a reality that was finally real.”​

​She looked at her husband, the clinical truth giving her a cold, unbreakable clarity.

​”It’s called structural dissociation. My brain fractured itself to keep me from shattering. It created a fantasy defense—an inner sanctuary with an imaginary guardian—because the alternative was total psychological death. My cognitive architecture was just trying to detect a protector in an empty room because it was hardwired to survive. It wasn’t the Holy Spirit visiting a thirteen-year-old girl; it was a traumatized ego deploying every defense mechanism it had left.”

​She let out a long, slow breath, her shoulders dropping as the ancient, cosmic guilt poured out of her.

​”I didn’t survive because of a miracle,” Dory said, looking her husband dead in the eye, finally claiming her own immense, terrifying strength. “My brain did what it had to do to keep that little girl in the wall bed from breaking. He didn’t keep me safe. I kept me safe. My own mind fought for me until I was strong enough to walk out of the dark and find a reality that was finally real.”

“They will tell you there is proof,” Dory said, her voice rising slightly, carrying the weight of decades of reading, researching, and trying to make the pieces fit. “Apologists point to the geography of the Levant as if a map is an validation of a miracle. They tell you to look at the Jordan River where Jesus was baptized, or the dry stones of Israel where he walked. They point to the gnarled, ancient roots of the Garden of Gethsemane where he wept before the crucifixion.”

​She gestured out the window, as if pointing to the thousands of libraries across the world. “I looked into it. I read their proofs. They will give you endless coordinates:

  • ​The Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem, where the blind man supposedly washed and gained his sight.
  • ​The rocky hill of Golgotha, the place of the skull, where the crosses physically stood.
  • ​The ancient town of Capernaum, the ruins of the synagogue where he cast out spirits.
  • ​The Sea of Galilee, a real, wind-swept body of water where fishermen cast their nets.
  • ​The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the very tomb they claim was left empty.

​They look at these real, physical places and say, ‘See? The setting is real, so the magic must be real too.’“

​Dory leaned forward, her fingers tapping the wooden table with a sharp, rhythmic finality. “But that is a flaw in elementary logic. Because if real geography proves a god, then every god on earth is alive.

​Look at the Indian subcontinent. The Ram Setu, the chain of limestone shoals stretching between the southern tip of India and Sri Lanka, is entirely real—visible from satellites, exactly where the ancient Hindu epics said Rama built a bridge to rescue his wife. If we travel across India, we find the pillars of Mahabalipuram, the sacred banks of the Varanasi Ghats along the Ganges where rituals have burned for millennia, the ancient caves of Kedarnath hidden high in the Himalayas, and the ruins of Ayodhya. If a physical landmark proves a theological claim, then the entire Hindu pantheon must be ruling the cosmos right now.

​And what of Islam? Mecca and Medina are absolute realities. The Kaaba stands in the center of the Grand Mosque, a physical focal point for billions. Millions of pilgrims march between the hills of Safa and Marwa, retracing the desperate search of Hagar for water. They gather at the Mount of Arafat, the very hill where Muhammad delivered his farewell sermon. They walk the plains of Mina and visit the ancient Well of Zamzam, which still flows with water today. By the same logic, the text of the Quran is validated purely because the sand and the stones are where they said they were.

​Go further east to Buddhism. The ancient Maha Bodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya stands precisely where Siddhartha Gautama sat under the Bodhi tree and achieved enlightenment. The ruins of the Jetavana monastery in Sravasti, where the Buddha spent most of his monastic life, are excavated and real. You can walk through Sarnath, the deer park where he preached his very first sermon, visit the Dhamekh Stupa built to mark the spot, and touch the stone ruins of Kushinagar, the physical place where he died.

​Even Jainism, rooted in deep antiquity, leaves an undeniable physical footprint. The massive stone temples of Dilwara are carved into the rocks of Mount Abu. The ancient monolithic statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola has stood for over a thousand years, carved out of a single granite hill. Pilgrims climb the rugged peaks of Shikharji, the holy mountain where twenty of the twenty-four Tirthankaras achieved liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

​Every single belief system has its landmarks,” Dory whispered, her eyes dark and steady. “Every religion has its rivers, its mountains, its footprints in the mud, and its ancient ruins. The geography is real because humans live in a real world. We build altars where we suffer, and we give divine names to the mountains we climb.

​But a real river does not mean a man walked on water. A real mountain does not mean a god spoke from a cloud. And the existence of Israel or Mecca or a bridge in the ocean doesn’t change the fact that when a child was screaming for help in a locked room, the sky was completely empty.”

Dory’s husband couldn’t muster to say anything reasonable or logical, to counter her but only stretched out his hands

around her waist

pulling her close,

leaning his head against hers and

mumbling the words

“Our father who art in heaven…”
